title: Design a fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used entry when full, supporting get and put in constant time.
shortTitle: Design an LRU Cache (Least Recently Used)
topicTitle: Design a fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used entry when ful

s1_definition.profdef: A Least Recently Used cache stores up to a fixed number of key-value entries and, when it is full and a new key arrives, evicts the entry that was accessed longest ago. The classic design combines a hash map for constant-time key lookup with a doubly linked list that orders entries by recency, moving an entry to the front on every access and evicting from the back. Both get and put run in constant time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps only the ten most recently viewed customer profiles on a fast desk, because the full archive is slow to fetch. Every time a clerk looks at a profile, she moves that folder to the front of the desk. When a new profile is needed and the desk is full, she removes the folder at the very back, the one nobody has touched for the longest time, to make room. A card index on the side tells her instantly where each folder sits, so she never has to search the desk.
s1_definition.oneliner: Hash map for instant lookup plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency — touch moves to front, eviction removes the back.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Least Recently Used cache stores up to a fixed number of key-value entries and, when it is full and a new key arrives, evicts the entry that was accessed longest ago. The classic design combines a hash map for constant-time key lookup with a doubly linked list that orders entries by recency, moving an entry to the front on every access and evicting from the back. Both get and put run in constant time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps only the ten most recently viewed customer profiles on a fast desk, because the full archive is slow to fetch. Every time a clerk looks at a profile, she moves that folder to the front of the desk. When a new profile is needed and the desk is full, she removes the folder at the very back, the one nobody has touched for the longest time, to make room. A card index on the side tells her instantly where each folder sits, so she never has to search the desk.

**One line to remember:** Hash map for instant lookup plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency — touch moves to front, eviction removes the back.

sections.s2_technical:
The challenge is doing both operations in constant time. A plain map gives constant lookup but no notion of recency order. A plain list gives order but linear search. Combining them solves both: the map points directly to the list node, so you find any entry instantly, and the doubly linked list maintains recency so you can reorder and evict in constant time.

Each node holds a key, a value, and previous and next pointers. On `get(key)`, you look up the node in the map; if present you unlink it from its current position and move it to the front, marking it most recently used, then return its value. On `put(key, value)`, if the key exists you update the value and move the node to the front; if it is new you create a node, add it to the front, and put it in the map, and if the size now exceeds capacity you remove the tail node, which is the least recently used, and delete its key from the map. Using sentinel head and tail nodes removes null checks and makes the unlink and insert logic clean.

A doubly linked list is essential, not a singly linked one, because eviction and reordering need to remove a node and splice its neighbours together in constant time, which requires knowing the previous node directly. With a singly linked list you would have to scan to find the predecessor, which is linear. This is precisely why the interview answer pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list.

A senior-level nuance is that Java's `LinkedHashMap` already implements this: constructed with access order true and with `removeEldestEntry` overridden, it is an LRU cache in a few lines. I mention that I would use `LinkedHashMap` or a library like Caffeine in production, but can implement the map-plus-doubly-linked-list by hand to show I understand the mechanics. For thread safety I would guard it or use a concurrent cache, since the hand-rolled version is not thread-safe.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India serves account balances to a high-traffic mobile app, and reading every balance from the database is too slow and expensive. We cache recently requested balances in memory, but memory is limited, so when the cache is full we must drop the balance that has not been requested for the longest time. This is exactly a Least Recently Used cache, because recency of access decides what to keep.

Problem 2 — The cache is on the hot path, so both reading a cached balance and inserting a new one must be constant time; a linear scan to find the stalest entry would defeat the purpose. The hash-map-plus-doubly-linked-list design gives constant time for both.

In our mini-project we build an `LruBalanceCache` of capacity two over account-to-balance entries. The demo puts Rajesh and Priya, reads Rajesh to make him recent, then puts a third account, forcing eviction of the least recently used entry, and logs each eviction.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: capacity two, put Rajesh one million, put Priya two hundred fifty thousand, get Rajesh, put a third account seventy five thousand, then two reads.

Step 1: Put Rajesh. A new node is created, added to the front, and recorded in the map. The list from front to back is Rajesh, then the tail sentinel.

Step 2: Put Priya. A new node added to the front. The list is now Priya, Rajesh. Rajesh is at the back, meaning least recently used.

Step 3: Get Rajesh. The map finds his node, and we move it to the front. The list becomes Rajesh, Priya, so now Priya is the least recently used at the back.

Step 4: Put the third account at seventy five thousand. It is new, so we add it to the front and the map. The size is now three, which exceeds capacity two, so we remove the tail node, which is Priya, the least recently used, and delete her key from the map. We log the eviction.

Step 5: Get Priya. She was evicted, so the map returns null.

Step 6: Get Rajesh. He is still present because touching him in step three kept him recent, so he survived the eviction. The cache correctly kept the most recently used entries.

```
[2026-10-26 23:24:01] INFO    Get SAV2001: 1000000
[2026-10-26 23:24:01] INFO      evicted LRU key CUR3001
[2026-10-26 23:24:01] INFO    Get CUR3001: null
[2026-10-26 23:24:01] INFO    Get SAV2001: 1000000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  put SAV2001   head ⇄ [SAV2001] ⇄ tail
  put CUR3001   head ⇄ [CUR3001] ⇄ [SAV2001] ⇄ tail
  get SAV2001   head ⇄ [SAV2001] ⇄ [CUR3001] ⇄ tail   (SAV2001 to front)
  put SAV2099   head ⇄ [SAV2099] ⇄ [SAV2001] ⇄ [CUR3001] ⇄ tail
                size 3 > cap 2 → evict tail.prev = CUR3001
                head ⇄ [SAV2099] ⇄ [SAV2001] ⇄ tail
  map: {SAV2099, SAV2001}   CUR3001 removed
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — LRU Cache (HashMap + Doubly Linked List) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Composite structure: HashMap for O(1) lookup + DLL for order │
  │  Sentinel head/tail nodes remove null-edge cases              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: cache only stores + evicts by recency                     │
  │  O: eviction policy could be swapped (LFU) without API change │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           LruBalanceCache             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - capacity: int                      │
  │  - map: Map<String,Node>             │  key → node
  │  - head, tail: Node                   │  sentinels
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + get(key): BigDecimal               │  O(1), moves to front
  │  + put(key, value): void              │  O(1), evicts if full
  │  - addFront / remove / moveToFront    │  DLL splice helpers
  └───────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                  │ contains many
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │           Node            │
  │  key, value, prev, next   │
  └───────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Entry recency ─────────────────────────

  [new put] → front (MRU)
  [get/update] → move to front (MRU)
  [size > cap] → remove tail.prev (LRU) → evicted

  ── Call Chain (put forcing eviction) ─────────────────────

  1. put(SAV2099, 75000) — new key
  2.   map.put; addFront(node)
  3.   size 3 > cap 2 → lru = tail.prev (CUR3001)
  4.   remove(lru); map.remove(lru.key)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Least Recently Used cache holds a fixed number of entries and, when it is full and a new key arrives, evicts the entry that was accessed longest ago. The challenge is making both get and put constant time, and the classic solution combines two structures. A hash map gives constant-time lookup from a key to its node, and a doubly linked list orders the nodes by recency, with the most recently used at the front and the least recently used at the back.

On a get, I look the key up in the map, and if it is present I unlink its node and move it to the front to mark it most recently used, then return the value. On a put, if the key already exists I update the value and move it to the front, and if it is new I add a node at the front and record it in the map; then if the size exceeds capacity I remove the tail node, which is the least recently used, and delete its key from the map. I use sentinel head and tail nodes so the splicing logic has no null edge cases. The list must be doubly linked, because removing a node and joining its neighbours in constant time needs a direct pointer to the previous node.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to cache account balances for a high-traffic mobile app. Reading every balance from the database was too slow and costly, so we kept recently requested balances in memory, and when the cache filled we dropped the balance nobody had asked for in the longest time. Both the cached read and the insert are constant time, which is essential on that hot path.

The senior-level point I make is that Java already ships this: a LinkedHashMap constructed in access order with removeEldestEntry overridden is an LRU cache in a handful of lines, and in production I would reach for that or a library like Caffeine, adding thread-safety since the hand-rolled version is not concurrent. I implement the map-plus-doubly-linked-list by hand in interviews to prove I understand the mechanics, but I always name the production-ready option too.
